The record:
Write the postmortem for the incident below.

Alert: HighErrorRate on io-shop
What the alert said [AL1]: Error rate above threshold for 5m {A1}
Alert raised: 2026-11-11T03:44:57Z {alert_raised}
Nobody was paged: no on-call incident was linked to this one. An alert rule fires; a person is paged. Argus first posted about the incident in Slack at 2026-11-11T03:45:21Z {first_told}, and the document says so already: leave that post out, and do not say that no person was told. That nobody was paged is a finding of its own.
The alert rule waits 5 minutes {rule_waits} with its condition holding before it fires. The alert came within the 7 minutes 30 seconds {accounted_for} accounted for by its rule waiting 5 minutes {rule_waits} with its condition holding, its evaluation at intervals of 1 minute {rule_evaluated_every}, an unmeasured allowance of 30 seconds {scraping_allowance} for scraping and storing its samples and the whole minute the onset is measured to.
Broken from 2026-11-11T03:38:00Z {began} (the onset, dated to its minute: a change came during that minute) to 2026-11-11T03:50:00Z {back_to_normal}, when the metrics show it back to normal.
That is 12 minutes {duration}, and every impact figure below is measured over that stretch.
Argus held the incident for 5 minutes 45 seconds {held}, until 2026-11-11T03:51:04Z {argus_stopped}. That is not how long the fault lasted, nor how long Argus went on working - leave it out of your answer.
The service's error rate over all its requests, before it began: 1.0% {errors_before}.
The same rate while it was broken: 29.2% {errors_while_broken}, peaking at 37.5% {errors_at_worst}.
Rise above baseline: 28.2% {errors_rise} of traffic failed that otherwise would not have.
The series behind the alert, `sum(rate(http_requests_total{code=~"5.."}[1m])) / sum(rate(http_requests_total[1m]))` - its alert said "Error rate above threshold for 5m {A1}" - which its alert rule evaluates and calls worse rising: 1.0166666666666666% {series_before} before it began, 29.16666666666667% {series_while_broken} on average while it was broken, and 37.5% {series_at_worst} at its worst. Say what it measures in words, not by its query.
Customer loss: 7,533.46 USD {customer_loss} - how far the shop's takings over the incident fell short of the same hours whole weeks earlier, beyond how much those hours vary on their own.

The switch-off is a weaker alternative and I can't fully exclude it.
  - [T16] 2026-11-11T03:46:36Z {T16.1} Argus: Read the flag provider's history - 2 {T16.2} flag changes by anyone but Argus, the 1 {T16.3} hour before 03:46:36 {T16.4}

  - [T26] 2026-11-11T03:49:47Z {T26.1} Mitigation Agent: Waiting to see whether the service is still at the incident's level, from 03:50 {T26.2} - up to 141s {T26.3}
  - [T27] 2026-11-11T03:51:04Z {T27.1} Mitigation Agent: Looked at the service - no longer at the incident's level since 03:50 {T27.2}

A person's message never stops a step already running: between steps, Argus starts no new one while a message waits to be answered.

Changes to production it read:
  - [P1] 2026-11-11T03:38:40Z {P1.1} flag-toggle legacy-checkout-fallback by admin: feature flag legacy-checkout-fallback was switched off
  - [P2] 2026-11-11T03:38:40Z {P2.1} flag-toggle monthly-spend-feature by admin: feature flag monthly-spend-feature was switched on
  - Deploys read, none came back.

Log lines it read, one per message:
  - [G153f] INFO io-shop: legacy-checkout-fallback=on - 200 {G153f.1} evaluations - 30 {G153f.2} occurrences in 30 {G153f.3} minutes, 03:08–03:37 {G153f.4}
  - [G7e5d] INFO io-shop: monthly-spend-feature=off - 200 {G7e5d.1} evaluations - 30 {G7e5d.2} occurrences in 30 {G7e5d.3} minutes, 03:08–03:37 {G7e5d.4}
  - [Gc27d] INFO io-shop: account pages served - # by the legacy renderer, # by the new renderer - 37 {Gc27d.1} occurrences in 37 {Gc27d.2} minutes, 03:08–03:44 {Gc27d.3}; # was 0 {Gc27d.4} to 200 {Gc27d.5}, typically 200 {Gc27d.6}, highest at 03:08 {Gc27d.7}; # was 0 {Gc27d.8} to 200 {Gc27d.9}, typically 0 {Gc27d.10}, highest at 03:39 {Gc27d.11}
  - [Gad41] INFO io-shop: account pages rendered normally - 4 {Gad41.1} occurrences in 22 {Gad41.2} minutes, 03:08–03:29 {Gad41.3}
  - [G46bc] ERROR io-shop: account page request failed - ClientDisconnected: the shopper closed the connection - 45 {G46bc.1} occurrences in 29 {G46bc.2} minutes, 03:09–03:37 {G46bc.3}
  - [Gbac1] WARN io-shop: account page error rate at #% over the last minute - 33 {Gbac1.1} occurrences in 36 {Gbac1.2} minutes, 03:09–03:44 {Gbac1.3}; # was 0.50% {Gbac1.4} to 37.50% {Gbac1.5}, typically 1.50% {Gbac1.6}, highest at 03:39 {Gbac1.7}
  - [G7ad6] INFO io-shop: legacy-checkout-fallback=off 60 {G7ad6.1} / on 140 {G7ad6.2} - 200 {G7ad6.3} evaluations - 1 {G7ad6.4} occurrence in 1 {G7ad6.5} minute, 03:38 {G7ad6.6}
  - [G971b] INFO io-shop: monthly-spend-feature=off 137 {G971b.1} / on 63 {G971b.2} - 200 {G971b.3} evaluations - 1 {G971b.4} occurrence in 1 {G971b.5} minute, 03:38 {G971b.6}
  - [G5309] ERROR io-shop: account page request failed - ZeroDivisionError: division by zero at src/io_shop/spend_summary.py:47 - 14 {G5309.1} occurrences in 7 {G5309.2} minutes, 03:38–03:44 {G5309.3}
  - [G7037] INFO io-shop: legacy-checkout-fallback=off - 200 {G7037.1} evaluations - 6 {G7037.2} occurrences in 6 {G7037.3} minutes, 03:39–03:44 {G7037.4}
  - [Gce95] INFO io-shop: monthly-spend-feature=on - 200 {Gce95.1} evaluations - 6 {Gce95.2} occurrences in 6 {Gce95.3} minutes, 03:39–03:44 {Gce95.4}

Candidates it considered, in the Investigator's words - name them by their labels, but cite none; what they claim is not what happened unless a row of the record shows it:
  - [C1] Feature flag monthly-spend-feature was switched on at 2026-11-11T03:38:40Z {C1.1}. Account pages then went through the new renderer, which raises ZeroDivisionError at src/io_shop/spend_summary.py:47, and the error rate stepped from about 1% {C1.2} to about 30% {C1.3}. Nothing was deployed and the rollout has converged. [feature-flag-toggle, confidence 0.8 {C1.4}, refuted]
  - [C2] Feature flag legacy-checkout-fallback was switched off at the same moment, which removed the legacy renderer path and exposed the failing new renderer. [feature-flag-toggle, confidence 0.15 {C2.1}, confirmed]

Actions it took:
  - [M1] Reverted the feature flag monthly-spend-feature for [C1] (can be put back) - refuted, put back when it did not help
  - [M2] Reverted the feature flag legacy-checkout-fallback for [C2] (can be put back) - confirmed, still in place

What Code-Fix read in the source and proposed, in Code-Fix's words - nothing ran its test or its fix, and what it claims is not what happened unless a row of the record shows it:
  - [F1] The fault: in `src/io_shop/spend_summary.py`, `average_spend_per_item_this_month` builds `bought_this_month` from the account's purchases flagged `in_current_month` and returns `account.total_this_month_cents // len(bought_this_month)`. When a shopper has bought nothing this month, that list is empty and the function raises ZeroDivisionError. The investigation's error points to that function: ZeroDivisionError at `src/io_shop/spend_summary.py:47`. `render_spend_summary` calls it whenever `use_monthly_summary` is true and `use_typical_spend` is false. `serve_account_page` in `src/io_shop/account_page.py` catches the exception and returns a failed page.
      
      Which flag was switched doesn't change this. The function cannot handle the most common kind of account, and it fails for every one of them whenever traffic reaches it. Because of that, the monthly figure can't safely be switched back on, and the legacy fallback can't safely be switched off, until the function itself is fixed. No flag named legacy-checkout-fallback appears anywhere in this repository. Whatever that flag does, it is evaluated outside this code. The only rollout switch here is the `use_monthly_summary` boolean the page is handed.
      
      The change: if nothing was bought this month, the function returns 0 {F1.1}, meaning nothing was spent per item this month. Otherwise it divides exactly as before. Shoppers who did buy this month get the same result as before. The lifetime average and `render_spend_summary` are unchanged. That includes the existing test that a shopper with no history at all still raises from the lifetime figure, so that failure still reaches the boundary.
      
      The test: `tests/io_shop/test_spend_summary.py` gains two cases. One asserts that the monthly average is 0 {F1.2} for an account with only earlier purchases. The other asserts that `render_spend_summary(..., use_monthly_summary=True)` returns 0 {F1.3} for the same kind of account. Against the current code, both cases would hit the division by zero.
  - Say what the files Code-Fix read do, with the conditions it gives - a default as a default, never as all it does - and no wider: 'nothing in the files it read', never 'nothing in the code'.

Action items the record already holds:
  - AI-1 (mitigate, done): Reverted the feature flag legacy-checkout-fallback
  - AI-2 (prevent, open): Review and merge the proposed fix
PR #550 is a draft Argus opened for a person to review and merge. The record holds nothing about it after that: do not say it was reviewed, approved or merged, or that it was not - nor that the record holds nothing, which the document says itself. Nothing ran its test or its fix: say what it proposes, not that it corrects anything.
The document already states what set it off, in a section of its own: the change [P1].

Cite evidence in causal_chain by its label. In a contributing factor's addressed_by, name the record's own action items that answer it, by their number; an item you propose names the factors it answers in its answers, by their labels.

What people working the incident wrote in its thread:
  - L1 (Some Person, 2026-11-11T03:45:45Z): "it's legacy-checkout-fallback - someone switched it off right before this started" - the investigation found it refuted: legacy-checkout-fallback was switched off at 2026-11-11T03:38:40Z, but monthly-spend-feature was switched on at the same moment, and the errors are ZeroDivisionError at src/io_shop/spend_summary.py:47 in the new renderer that flag enables. The switch-off is a weaker alternative and I can't fully exclude it.
Each was weighed on what the investigation had read, before anything was tried. Where the actions above say otherwise, the actions are the later word.
For each, say in lead_effects whether it changed what was done.

Call submit_postmortem with your answer.

The document, by field:
root_cause: Once account pages went through the new renderer, its monthly spend summary called average_spend_per_item_this_month in src/io_shop/spend_summary.py. That function divides the month's total by the number of purchases made this month and has no guard for an empty list. So it raises ZeroDivisionError for every shopper who has bought nothing this month, and serve_account_page turns that into a failed page. It rests on F1, a reading of the source nothing ran, so it is unverified.
cause_in_plain_words: Switching off an older fallback sent shoppers' account pages through a newer way of building them, and that newer way likely breaks for any shopper who has bought nothing this month, because it divides by that month's number of purchases.
still_at_risk: Switching the legacy checkout fallback off again, or anything else that sends account pages to the new renderer, could make account pages fail again for shoppers who have bought nothing this month.
symptom: Shoppers' account pages failed to load
lead_effects L1: It did not change what was done first: the investigation weighed it as refuted and Argus reverted monthly-spend-feature first, and the flag the lead named was switched back on only as the second candidate, which turned out to be the action that put the service back.
causal_chain 1: Shoppers' account page requests failed far more often than before. (cites Gbac1, under "Log lines it read, one per message"; G5309, under "Log lines it read, one per message")
causal_chain 2: The failed requests broke on a division-by-zero error raised while the page's spend summary was being built. (cites G5309, under "Log lines it read, one per message")
causal_chain 3: The error came from the new renderer, which had started serving account pages that the legacy renderer had served until then. (cites Gc27d, under "Log lines it read, one per message"; G5309, under "Log lines it read, one per message")
causal_chain 4: Pages moved to the new renderer because the feature flag legacy-checkout-fallback was switched off. (cites P1, under "Changes to production it read"; G7ad6, under "Log lines it read, one per message"; G7037, under "Log lines it read, one per message")
causal_chain 4 ruled_out 1: The switch-on of the feature flag monthly-spend-feature at the same instant (P2): the service stayed at the incident's level with it turned off again, and it was back to normal with it on once the fallback was restored. (cites T21, under "What Argus did, in order"; T22, under "What Argus did, in order"; T27, under "What Argus did, in order"; T28, under "What Argus did, in order")
causal_chain 5: The new renderer's monthly per-item spend average divides by zero, and the reading of the code puts this down to shoppers with no purchases this month. (cites G5309, under "Log lines it read, one per message"; F1, under "What Code-Fix read in the source and proposed, in Code-Fix's words - nothing ran its test or its fix")
contributing_factors 1: The legacy fallback was switched off for all account-page traffic at once. No check was seen that the path it exposed, the new renderer, worked first, and no staged rollout was seen.
contributing_factors 1 had_it_been_otherwise: A gradual switch-off, halted on rising errors, would have stopped the failure while only a small part of shoppers had reached the new renderer.
contributing_factors 2: Two feature flags were changed at the same instant, so the investigation could not tell their effects apart and blamed the wrong flag first.
contributing_factors 2 had_it_been_otherwise: Separate changes would have pointed straight at the fallback switch-off, so the first revert would have been the one that worked and the service would have recovered sooner.
contributing_factors 3: No test was seen for the monthly spend average with a shopper who has bought nothing this month.
contributing_factors 3 had_it_been_otherwise: Such a test would have exposed the division by zero before the new renderer took account-page traffic.
contributing_factors 4: The error-rate alert on io-shop paged nobody: no on-call incident was linked to it.
contributing_factors 4 had_it_been_otherwise: An on-call person would have been engaged from the alert, ready to act on the thread's lead if the automated reverts had not restored the service.
action_items 1: Roll out changes to io-shop feature flags gradually, with an automatic halt and revert when the error rate rises.
action_items 2: Require production flag changes on io-shop to be made one at a time, with a pause to watch errors between them.
action_items 3: Route the io-shop error-rate alert to the on-call rotation so that it pages a person.
went_wrong 1: The Investigator weighed the thread's lead as refuted and ranked the monthly-spend-feature switch-on first, so the first revert targeted the wrong flag and the flag the lead named was restored only on the second try.

Not to be judged:
  - Names in braces, such as {T5.1} or {duration}, are figures code writes in from the row they name. They are not judged.
  - Action items propose what to do; they make no claim about the record.
  - Whether something went well, went wrong or was lucky is a judgement. Only a fact it states is judged.

Judge every claim in the document, and answer by calling judge_claims.

tools.description: Submit every claim in the document, each either as supported or as flagged. Supported: the document's own words, quoted exactly, and the record's rows that support it. Flagged: the document's own words, quoted exactly, why, and the record's rows that contradict it (none where no row speaks to it at all). Empty lists say the document makes no claim to judge.

why.description: One sentence: what the record holds instead. Never empty.
